content: The medication atropine sulfate, often used in ophthalmic preparations, is primarily indicated for use before eye examinations, such as refraction tests, and for the treatment of certain eye conditions, including uveitis. It belongs to a class of drugs known as anticholinergics, which work by inhibiting the action of acetylcholine at parasympathetic sites in smooth muscle, the central nervous system (CNS), and secretory glands. When applying atropine eye ointment, it is essential to wash your hands thoroughly beforehand. To avoid contamination, do not touch the tip of the tube to your eye or any other surface. Tilt your head back, look upward, and gently pull down the lower eyelid to create a small pouch. Squeeze a strip of ointment (approximately 0.5 cm) into the pouch, close your eye gently, and roll your eyeball in all directions to distribute the medication evenly. If you are using other eye medications, such as drops or ointments, wait at least 5–10 minutes before applying the next medication. For optimal benefit, use the medication at the same time(s) each day if prescribed on a regular schedule. Common side effects of atropine eye ointment include burning, stinging, redness, eye irritation, or temporary blurred vision. These effects are usually mild and temporary. However, if you experience severe or persistent symptoms, contact your healthcare provider. Serious allergic reactions to this medication are rare but may occur. If you notice symptoms of a severe allergic reaction, such as rash, itching, swelling, severe dizziness, or difficulty breathing, seek immediate medical attention. Before using atropine, inform your doctor or pharmacist if you are allergic to it, to other belladonna alkaloids (e.g., hyoscyamine, scopolamine), or if you have any other allergies. This product may contain inactive ingredients that could cause allergic reactions or other problems. After applying the medication, your vision may become temporarily blurred, and your eyes may be more sensitive to light. Protect your eyes in bright light by wearing sunglasses if necessary. Infants and small children may be more sensitive to the side effects of this drug, so take extra precautions to prevent the medication from entering a child’s mouth. During pregnancy, atropine should only be used when clearly needed, as there is limited data on its safety in pregnant women. It is unknown whether this drug passes into breast milk, so consult your doctor before breastfeeding. Atropine may interact with other medications, potentially altering their effects or increasing the risk of side effects. Keep a list of all the products you use, including prescription and non-prescription drugs and herbal supplements, and share it with your healthcare provider. If you suspect an overdose and experience serious symptoms such as passing out or difficulty breathing, call emergency services immediately (911 in the U.S.). For non-emergency cases, contact a poison control center (1-800-222-1222 in the U.S. or 1-844-764-7669 in Canada). Store this medication at room temperature, away from light and moisture. Do not freeze it. Properly discard the product when it is expired or no longer needed. Do not flush medications down the toilet or pour them into a drain unless instructed to do so. This information is a summary and does not include all possible details about this product. It is not a substitute for professional medical advice. Always consult your healthcare provider for complete information about this medication and your specific health needs.
